rows: White-tailed deer have two kinds of colour-sensing cells, where people have three. Reds and oranges look yellow or grey to them.

Reindeer grazing with their eyes turned level are given a combined field of about 360 degrees along the ground, and horses a field of about 320. Nobody has measured the field of a white-tailed deer, so you very likely see most of the way around you without turning your head.

Grazing animals have pupils shaped like horizontal bars. The shape widens their view along the ground and cuts glare from the sky. It also smears out-of-focus things sideways, and this view does the same.
These parts of the view are guesses. This view treats things lower in the picture as closer.

rows: If you are a white-tailed deer, you have one cone most sensitive at 450 to 460 nanometers and one at 537. A human has three kinds, and you have two. Blues and yellow-greens stay apart for you, and orange and red can still be told from them.

If you are a white-tailed deer, the finest detail you resolve lies between 4 and 6 cycles per degree. A human reads about 30 on an eye chart. Fences, faces and the edges of a dark shape blur at a distance where a human still sees them clearly.
If you are a white-tailed deer, your pupil is a horizontal slit. A reindeer's pupil in bright light is also a bar stretched sideways.
If you are a white-tailed deer, your cones that answer to middle wavelengths crowd into a horizontal streak across the retina. A level band of your view is sharper than the rest.

A reindeer grazing with its eyes turned to a horizontal position has a combined field of about 360 degrees parallel to the ground, and the same is said of deer generally. You very likely see almost all the way round without turning your head.
If you are a white-tailed deer, a reflecting layer behind your retina sends light back through it. Your eyes are specialized for the low light of dawn and dusk, when you are most active.

A reindeer's eye lets some ultraviolet through, and its dark-adapted eyes detect light from 330 to 410 nanometers. Deer in general are very likely sensitive to wavelengths shorter than 400. You very likely see bluish and bright surfaces with a hint of ultraviolet.

Nobody has measured how much sharper your streak is than the edge of your view, or how steeply the blur grows away from it. Nobody has measured how much the reflecting layer lifts a dim scene, or how much of a bluish surface reaches you as ultraviolet. Those amounts, and the way your two cone peaks turn into colors, are guesses.
Nobody has measured some parts of how you see, so they are guesses.
White-tailed deer have two kinds of colour-sensing cells, where people have three. Reds and oranges look yellow or gray to them.

Grazing animals have pupils shaped like horizontal bars. The shape widens their view along the ground and cuts glare from the sky. It also smears out-of-focus things sideways, and this view does the same.
These parts of the view are guesses. This view treats things lower in the picture as closer.
On this trial the colours come from the measured receptor peaks (455, 537 nm). The camera's colours and the display are the app's.
Jacobs, Deegan and Neitz 1994, white-tailed deer
As the light falls, the colours drift toward what the rods take in, which peak near 497 nm. The peak is measured; where the change happens is the app's guess.

A deer sees in dim light partly by pooling light over time. With &draw=exposure, in the dark the picture pools the last few seconds, so still things settle and moving things leave ghosts. The pooling time is the app's.

rows.title: Color
rows.text: If you are a white-tailed deer, you have two kinds of color-sensing cell, one most sensitive to blue light and one most sensitive to green, where a human has three. The fallow deer has the same two, and if you are another deer, a sheep or a bison, you very likely have two kinds as well.
rows.note: Jacobs 1994 measured both deer: a blue cell shared by both (450 to 460 nm) and a green cell (537 nm in the white-tailed deer, 542 in the fallow deer). Carried within the hoofed animals by the photopigment rule; the horse is left out as another order.
rows.rewrite_reason: Draft implies white-tailed deer have only a blue cell and fallow deer only a green one; one study measured both deer. Lead with deer.

rows.title: Field of view
rows.text: Your eyes sit on the sides of your head, and a book on deer says they let you watch almost a complete circle, about 310 degrees. The book does not say how that was found, and nobody has measured how much of the space around you both of your eyes see at once. In goats, which are not deer, a review states a field of 320 to 340 degrees, with 20 to 60 degrees seen by both eyes together.

cites.taxon: Cervidae (deer, as the page states it)

rows.note: No deer record measures field or binocular overlap; R10 is a book statement with no stated method, so it is attributed to the book. Goat figures are named as goat figures only.

rows.title: Pupil
rows.text: Your pupil is a slit lying on its side, wider than it is tall. It has been recorded this way in white-tailed deer, red deer, moose, reindeer, pudu and gray brocket. If you are a reindeer, the slit measures about 25 square millimeters when narrowed, and the pupil opens to a round shape of about 335 square millimeters when dilated.
rows.note: Removed the "13 times larger" figure, which was my own division and not in a record. No record gives the pupil of mule deer, roe deer or fallow deer, so the row names only the measured deer.

rows.title: Sharpness, dim light and depth
rows.text: If you are a white-tailed deer, you see a fifth or less of the fine detail a human sees, and a light-reflecting layer called the tapetum lucidum covers the upper part of your eye and overlaps the horizontal strip where you see most sharply. A review of deer eyes states that deer in general have this layer, so other deer very likely have it too. Nobody has measured how dim a light you can see by, and nobody has tested how you judge depth.
rows.note: Dim-light sensitivity and depth cue have no deer records (only horse, sheep, cattle), so both are stated as unmeasured. Replaced "reports" with "states" for the voice check.
